moonLanding.title: Moon Landing Simulator
moonLanding.subtitle: Use thrust and attitude control to touch down inside the safe landing envelope.
moonLanding.instructions: W/S changes throttle. A/D rotates. Reduce vertical and horizontal speed before contact.
moonLanding.learnBody: Gravity continuously accelerates the lander downward. Thrust changes acceleration; burning fuel reduces mass, so the same thrust gradually produces more acceleration.
moonLanding.retry: Adjust your approach and try again.
moonLanding.experimentCopy: Change starting conditions, apply them, then compare the resulting descent.
moonLanding.hardReason: The lander survived, but impact velocity or tilt exceeded the safe landing envelope.
moonLanding.crashReason: Impact energy was too high. Reduce descent speed and stabilize before contact.
moonLanding.safeReason: Touchdown stayed inside the safe velocity and orientation envelope.

objectives: Observe how fuel burn changes total mass
Land inside a safe velocity and attitude envelope

faq.a: The lander must continuously manage downward acceleration while preserving enough fuel to reduce velocity before contact.

faq.q: Why does acceleration change as fuel burns?
faq.a: Burning fuel reduces spacecraft mass. With the same thrust, lower mass produces greater acceleration because a = F/m.

faq.q: What counts as a safe landing here?
faq.a: The simulation checks vertical speed, horizontal speed and lander orientation at surface contact.

seo.related: Gravity · thrust · acceleration · mass · rocket equation

orbitalRescue.title: Orbital Rescue Simulator
orbitalRescue.subtitle: Match a target satellite's orbit using real Newtonian gravity and finite propellant.
orbitalRescue.instructions: Choose a burn direction and throttle. Prograde raises orbital energy; retrograde lowers it. Rendezvous requires both low distance and low relative velocity.
orbitalRescue.learnBody: A prograde burn increases orbital energy. A retrograde burn decreases it. Changing speed changes the shape of the orbit rather than simply moving the spacecraft straight up or down.
orbitalRescue.experimentCopy: Change starting conditions and compare how identical burns alter the resulting orbit.
orbitalRescue.rescuedReason: Rendezvous achieved with low distance and low relative velocity.
orbitalRescue.reentryReason: Perigee fell too low and the spacecraft reentered.
orbitalRescue.escapedReason: The spacecraft moved beyond the mission region.

objectives: Relate altitude to circular orbital velocity
Use prograde and retrograde burns to change orbital energy
Rendezvous by reducing both distance and relative velocity

faq.q: Why does a prograde burn raise the orbit?
faq.a: Adding velocity increases specific orbital energy and typically raises the opposite side of the orbit.

faq.q: Why is matching position not enough for rescue?
faq.a: Rendezvous also requires low relative velocity. Two spacecraft can pass very close while moving too differently to dock safely.

faq.q: Is the orbit a predefined animation?
faq.a: No. Position and trajectory are generated from Newtonian gravity and the player’s applied thrust.

learn.title: Learn the science behind the controls
learn.subtitle: Start with intuition, then reveal the math when you want it.
learn.gravityBody: Gravity changes velocity continuously. Near the Moon's surface the acceleration is about 1.62 m/s².
learn.thrustBody: Thrust is a force. Acceleration depends on both thrust and current spacecraft mass: a = F/m.
learn.orbitBody: An orbit is continuous free fall. At a given radius, circular orbital speed is v = √(GM/r).
learn.rocketBody: Finite propellant limits maneuvering. Available delta-v follows Δv = Isp × g0 × ln(m0/mf).
